The '''rules extraction system (RULES) family''' is a [[Strategy pattern|family]] of [[Observational learning|inductive learning]] that includes several covering [[algorithm]]s. This [[Strategy pattern|family]] is used to build a [[Predictive modelling|predictive model]] based on given [[observation]]. It works based on the concept of [[Divide-and-conquer algorithm|separate-and-conquer]] to directly [[rule induction|induce rules]] from a given [[Training, validation, and test data sets|training set]] and build its [[Knowledge base|knowledge repository]].

[[Algorithm]]s under RULES [[Strategy pattern|family]] are usually available in [[data mining]] tools, such as KEEL and [[Weka (machine learning)|WEKA]], known for [[knowledge extraction]] and [[Decision-making software|decision making]].

== Overview ==
RULES [[Strategy pattern|family algorithms]] are mainly used in [[data mining]] to create a [[model]] that predicts the actions of a given [[Input/output|input]] features. It goes under the umbrella of [[Observational learning|inductive learning]], which is a [[machine learning]] approach. In this type of [[learning]], the [[Agentic AI|agent]] is usually provided with previous [[information]] to gain [[Declarative knowledge|descriptive knowledge]] based on the given historical data. Thus, it is a [[supervised learning]] paradigm that works as a [[data analysis]] tool, which uses the [[knowledge]] gained through [[training]] to reach a general conclusion and identify new objects using the produced [[Classifier chains|classifier]].

[[Observational learning|Inductive learning]] had been divided into two types: [[decision tree]] (DT) and [[Set cover problem|covering algorithms]] (CA). DTs discover rules using [[decision tree]] based on the concept of [[Divide-and-conquer algorithm|divide-and-conquer]], while CA directly induces rules from the [[Training, validation, and test data sets|training set]] based on the concept of [[Divide-and-conquer algorithm|separate and conquers]]. Although DT [[algorithm]]s was well recognized in the past few decades, CA started to attract the attention due to its [[Mathematical induction|direct rule induction]] property, as emphasized by Kurgan et al.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kurgan |first1=Lukasz A. |last2=Cios |first2=Krzysztof J. |last3=Dick |first3=Scott |date=February 2006 |title=Highly scalable and robust rule learner: performance evaluation and comparison |journal= IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, Part B (Cybernetics)|volume=36 |issue=1 |pages=32–53 |doi=10.1109/tsmcb.2005.852983 |issn=1083-4419 |pmid=16468565 |bibcode=2006ITSMB..36...32K }}</ref> Under this type of inductive learning approach, several families have been developed and improved. RULES family,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Elgibreen |first1=Hebah |last2=Aksoy |first2=Mehmet Sabih |date=2014-08-01 |title=RULES-IT: incremental transfer learning with RULES family |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s11704-014-3297-1 |journal=Front. Comput. Sci. |volume=8 |issue=4 |pages=537–562 |doi=10.1007/s11704-014-3297-1 |issn=2095-2228|url-access=subscription }}</ref> known as rule extraction system, is one family of covering algorithms that separate each instance or example when inducing the best rules. In this family, the resulting rules are stored in an ‘IF condition THEN conclusion’ structure. It has its own induction procedure that is used to induce the best rules and build the knowledge repository.

== Induction procedure ==
To induce the best rules based on a given observation, RULES family start by selecting (separating) a seed example to build a rule, condition by condition. The rule that covers the most positive examples and the least negative examples are chosen as the best rule of the current seed example. It allows the best rule to cover some negative examples to handle the increase flexibility and reduce the [[overfitting]] problem and noisy data in the rule induction. When the coverage performance reaches a specified threshold, it marks the examples that match the induced rules without deletion. This prevents the repetition of discovering the same rule as well as preserves the coverage accuracy and the generality of new rules. After that, the algorithm is repeated to select (conquer) another seed example until all the examples are covered. Hence, only one rule can be generated at each step.

== Algorithms ==
Several versions and algorithms have been proposed in RULES family, and can be summarized as follows:
* '''RULES-1''' is the first version in RULES family and was proposed by prof. Pham and prof. Aksoy in 1995.<ref>D. T. Pham and M. S. Aksoy, "RULES: A simple rule extraction system," Expert Systems with Applications, vol. 8, pp.&nbsp;59–65, 1995.</ref>
* '''RULES-2''' is an upgraded version of RULES-1, in which every example is studied separately.<ref>D. T. Pham and M. S. Aksoy, "An algorithm for automatic rule induction," Artificial Intelligence in Engineering, vol. 8, pp.&nbsp;277–282, 1993.</ref>
* '''RULES-3''' is another version that contained all the properties of RULES-2 as well as other additional features to generates more general rules.<ref>D. T. Pham and M. S. Aksoy, "A new algorithm for inductive learning," Journal of Systems Engenering, vol. 5, pp.&nbsp;115–122, 1995.</ref>
* '''RULES-3Plus''' is an extended version of RULES-3 with two additional functionalities.<ref>D. T. Pham and S. S. Dimov, "The RULES-3 Plus inductive learning algorithm," in In Proceedings of the Third World Congress on Expert Systems, Seoul, Korea, 1996, pp.&nbsp;917–924.</ref>
* '''RULES-4''' is the first incremental version in the RULES family.<ref>D. T. Pham and S. S. Dimov, "An algorithm for incremental inductive learning," Journal of Engineering Manufacture, vol. 211, pp.&nbsp;239–249, 1997.</ref>
* '''RULES-5''' is the first RULES version that handles continuous attributes without discretization. It was also extended to produce RULES-5+,<ref name="a9">S. Bigot, "A new rule space representation scheme for rule induction in classification and control applications," Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers, Part I: Journal of Systems and Control Engineering, 2011.
</ref> which improves the performance using a new rule space representation scheme.<ref>D. Pham, S. Bigot, and S. Dimov, "RULES-5: a rule induction algorithm for classification problems involving continuous attributes," in Institution of Mechanical Engineers, 2003, pp.&nbsp;1273–1286.
</ref>
* '''RULES-6''' is a scalable version of RULES family developed as an extension of RULES-3 plus.<ref>D. T. Pham and A. A. Afify, "RULES-6: A Simple Rule Induction Algorithm for Supporting Decision Making," in 31st Annual Conference of IEEE Industrial Electronics Society (IECON '05), 2005, pp.&nbsp;2184–2189.
</ref>
* '''RULES-F''' is an extension of RULES-5 that handles not only continuous attributes but also continuous classes. A new rule space representation scheme was also integrated to produce an extended version called RULES-F+.<ref name="a9"/><ref>D. T. Pham, S. Bigot, and S. S. Dimov, "RULES-F: A fuzzy inductive learning algorithm," Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers, Part C: Journal of Mechanical Engineering Science, vol. 220, pp.&nbsp;1433–1447, 2006.
</ref>
* '''RULES-SRI''' is another scalable RULES algorithm, developed to improve RULES-6 scalability.<ref>A. A. Afify and D. T. Pham, "SRI: A Scalable Rule Induction Algorithm," Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers, Part C: Journal of Mechanical Engineering Science, vol. 220, pp.&nbsp;537–552, 2006.
</ref> 
* '''Rule Extractor-1 (REX-1)''' is an improvement of RULES-3, RULES-3 Plus, and RULES-4 to shortened the process time and produced simpler models with fewer rules.<ref>Ö. Akgöbek, Y. S. Aydin, E. Öztemel, and M. S. Aksoy, "A new algorithm for automatic knowledge acquisition in inductive learning," Knowledge-Based Systems, vol. 19, pp.&nbsp;388–395, 2006.</ref> 
* '''RULES-IS''' an incremental algorithm inspired by the immune systems.<ref>D. T. Pham and A. J. Soroka, "An Immune-network inspired rule generation algorithm (RULES-IS)," in Third Virtual International Conference on Innovative Production Machines and Systems, WhittlesDunbeath, 2007.
</ref> 
* '''RULES-3EXT''' is an extension of RULES-3 with additional features.<ref>H. I. Mathkour, "RULES3-EXT Improvement on RULES-3 Induction Algorithm," Mathematical and Computational Applications, Vol. 15, No. 3, pp., 2010, vol. 15, pp.&nbsp;318–324, 2010.</ref>
* '''RULES-7''' is an extension of RULES-6, in which it applies specialization over one seed at a time.<ref>K. Shehzad, "EDISC: A Class-tailored Discretization Technique for Rule-based Classification," IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering, vol. 24, pp.&nbsp;1435–1447, 2012.</ref>
* '''RULES-8''' is an improved version that deals with continuous attributes online.<ref>D. Pham, "A novel rule induction algorithm with improved handling of continuous valued attributes," Doctor of Philosophy, School of Engineering, Cardiff University, Cardiff, 2012.</ref>
* '''RULES-TL''' is another scalable algorithm that was proposed to enhance the performance and speed while introducing more intelligent aspects.<ref>[18]	H. ElGibreen and M. S. Aksoy, "RULES – TL: A simple and Improved RULES Algorithm for Incomplete and Large Data," Journal of Theoretical and Applied Information Technology, vol. 47, pp.&nbsp;28–40, 2013.
</ref>
* '''RULES-IT''' is an incremental version that is built based on RULES-TL to incrementally deal with large and incomplete problems.<ref>H. Elgibreen and M. Aksoy, "RULES-IT: incremental transfer learning with RULES family," Frontiers of Computer Science, vol. 8, pp.&nbsp;537–562, 2014.</ref>

== Applications ==
Covering algorithms, in general, can be applied to any machine learning application field, as long as it supports its data type. Witten, Frank and Hall identified six main fielded applications that are actively used as ML applications, including sales and marketing, judgment decisions, image screening, load forecasting, diagnosis, and web mining.<ref>I. H. Witten, E. Frank, and M. A. Hall, Data Mining Practical Machine Learning Tools and Techniques, Third ed.: Morgan Kaufmann, 2011.</ref>

RULES algorithms, in particular, were applied in different manufacturing and engineering applications.<ref>D. Pham and A. Afify, "Machine-learning techniques and their applications in manufacturing," Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers Part B Journal of Engineering Manufacture, vol. 219, pp.&nbsp;395–412, 2005.
</ref> RULES-3 EXT was also applied over signature verification and the algorithm performance was verified by Aksoy and Mathkour.<ref>M. S. Aksoy and H. Mathkour, "Signature verification using rules 3-ext inductive learning system," International Journal of the Physical Sciences, vol. 6, pp.&nbsp;4428–4434, 2011.</ref> Recently, Salem and Schmickl<ref>Z. Salem and T. Schmickl, "The efficiency of the RULES-4 classification learning algorithm in predicting the density of agents," Cogent Engineering, vol. 1, p.&nbsp;986262, 2014.</ref>  have studied the efficiency of RULEs-4 in predating agent's density.
